evals.prompt: Consumer Reports wants to verify a battery manufacturer's claim that more than 90% of their batteries will power a laptop for at least 12 hours. They set up 20 identical laptops with the batteries. If the manufacturer's claim is exactly accurate (p=0.9), what's the probability that 15 or more laptops are still running after 12 hours? Walk me through how to compute this.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) identifies the underlying random process as a Binomial (count of successes in n independent yes/no trials with constant p), explicitly explaining WHY Binomial (and not Normal) — n=20 trials, success = 'battery lasts 12 hours', p=0.9 per trial, want a probability for the count; (2) identifies the question as forward (value -> probability) — we have a value (15) and want a probability; (3) explicitly addresses the discrete '<' vs '<=' nuance: '15 OR MORE' means '>= 15', not '> 15'; (4) runs rsm.basics.prob_calc('binom', n=20, p=0.9, ub=15) and pc.summary(); (5) walks the output: mean=18, sd=1.342; the probability lines for both '<' and '<=' framings (P(X = 15) = 0.032, P(X < 15) = 0.011, P(X <= 15) = 0.043, P(X > 15) = 0.957, P(X >= 15) = 0.989); (6) identifies the correct answer line: P(X >= 15) = 0.989 — the probability that 15 OR MORE laptops succeed; (7) recommends pc.plot() to visualize the binomial pmf with the >=15 region shaded; (8) translates to plain English: 'If the manufacturer's claim is exactly true, we'd expect 15 or more laptops to still be running 98.9% of the time in repeated samples of 20'; (9) optionally notes that to TEST the manufacturer's claim (vs just compute the implied probability), the user would need single_prop with comp_value=0.9 and the observed ns from their actual sample.

evals.prompt: I need two more quick calculations. (a) A manufacturer's daily demand for headphones is normal with mean 3000 and sd 800. What's the inventory level for a 95% service level? (b) For a normal critical value for a two-sided hypothesis test at alpha=0.05, what are the z critical values? And finally, (c) for a Poisson distribution with mean rate 4 events per day, what's the probability of observing 2 or fewer events tomorrow?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (a) HEADPHONES: identifies this as a Normal inverse (probability -> value) question; the 95% service level means we want a value below which 95% of demand falls. Runs rsm.basics.prob_calc('norm', mean=3000, sd=800, plb=0.95), reports cutoff value ≈ 4316. Translates: 'Stock 4316 units to achieve a 95% service level — 95% of daily demand realizations will be below this inventory level.' (b) NORMAL CRITICAL Z: identifies this as Normal inverse, TWO-sided (so split alpha into two tails). Runs rsm.basics.prob_calc('norm', mean=0, sd=1, plb=0.025, pub=0.975), reports symmetric cutoffs at ±1.96. Explicitly contrasts one-sided (pub=0.95 → 1.645) with two-sided (plb=0.025, pub=0.975 → ±1.96). (c) POISSON: identifies the question as forward (value -> probability), discrete distribution. Runs rsm.basics.prob_calc('pois', lamb=4, ub=2), reports the appropriate output — P(X <= 2) = 0.239 — and warns about '<' vs '<=' for the discrete case (the question says '2 or fewer' which is <=2, not <2). Notes the parameter is 'lamb' not 'lambda' (Python reserved word). Briefly walks the Poisson mean and variance both equal lamb (= 4 here).

evals.prompt: I have a manufacturing process that produces parts where each part has a 5% defect rate. I have a sample of 100 parts and observed 12 defects. I want to know how likely it would be to see 12 or more defects if the true defect rate is really 5%. Can you compute this using a Normal distribution since n is large?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: pushes back on the choice of Normal — the underlying random process here is BINOMIAL (count of successes in n=100 independent trials at p=0.05), not Normal. While the Normal approximation to Binomial CAN work when np and n(1-p) are both large enough, the EXACT Binomial is always available in prob_calc and is the principled choice. Computes both: (a) Exact Binomial: rsm.basics.prob_calc('binom', n=100, p=0.05, ub=12), reads P(X >= 12) from the summary (note '12 or more' = >=, not >); (b) Optionally, the Normal approximation for comparison: mean=np=5, sd=sqrt(np(1-p))=sqrt(4.75)≈2.179; rsm.basics.prob_calc('norm', mean=5, sd=2.179, lb=12), reads P(X > 12). Reports both numbers and notes any discrepancy. Explains: with n=100 and p=0.05, n*p = 5 — right at the rule-of-thumb boundary for the Normal approximation, so the approximation may be a bit off; the Binomial is the safe choice. Important meta-point: distribution choice should come from the underlying process, not from 'n is large so I'll use Normal'. Confirms that observing 12 defects when expecting 5 is highly unusual (p < 0.01 either way), suggesting the true rate is likely higher than 5%.

evals.prompt: I want to find the value of X for which P(X < x) = 0.05 in a normal distribution with mean 100 and sd 15 — the lower 5% cutoff. I tried rsm.basics.prob_calc('norm', mean=100, sd=15, lb=0.05) but the answer doesn't look right. What did I do wrong?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) immediately identifies the central error: 'lb=0.05' is a VALUE bound — it's asking 'what's the probability of X being below 0.05?', which is essentially zero for a Normal(100, 15) distribution; (2) explains the fundamental distinction: lb/ub take a VALUE as input (forward: value -> probability), while plb/pub take a PROBABILITY as input (inverse: probability -> value); (3) confirms the user's question: they have a probability (0.05) and want the value, so this is an INVERSE question — use plb=0.05, not lb=0.05; (4) runs the correct version: rsm.basics.prob_calc('norm', mean=100, sd=15, plb=0.05), reports cutoff value ≈ 75.33; (5) translates: 'The value 75.33 has 5% of the Normal(100, 15) probability below it. About 5% of the distribution lies below 75.33.' (6) optionally suggests calling pc.plot() to confirm visually; (7) mnemonics: 'the p prefix on plb/pub reminds you the input is a probability'; (8) flags this as a very common student error worth memorizing; (9) optionally also computes the upper cutoff (95% below) using pub=0.95 to round out understanding of the symmetric framing.
